input.text:
Further, a prior analysis of the present sample examined whether the momentary negative affect-binge eating association was mediated by negative urgency (i.e., a self-regulatory process that overlaps with emotion dysregulation [r = 0.948 in the present study] and is defined as behaving impulsively while experiencing negative affect; Wonderlich et al. [2024]).

Results. Characteristics for the present sample (N = 107) are reported in Table 1. Participants responded to 3131 out of 4494 possible surveys, reflecting good compliance (70.00%). Most participants identified as women (n = 88, 82.24%) and White (n = 99, 92.52%). On average, participants were 39.87 (SD = 13.35) years old and had a BMI of 35.10 (SD = 8.67). Further, participants generally reported LOC eating at a moderate level of severity across the assessed dimensions, yet with high variability (all ranges = 1-5): (1) general feeling of losing control while eating (M = 2.26, SD = 1.32); (2) difficulties resisting eating (M = 2.79, SD = 1.42); (3) difficulties stopping eating after starting (M = 2.54, SD = 1.41); (4) feeling driven or compelled to eat (M = 2.88, SD = 1.38); (5) not paying attention to one's eating (M = 3.45, SD = 1.18); (6) feeling disconnected while eating (M = 2.19, SD = 1.26).

Regarding the direct effects, across models, there were significant positive associations between the negative affect and emotion dysregulation latent factors at the within-person (b = 0.24) and between-person (b = 0.90) levels, and inverse associations between the positive affect and emotion dysregulation factors at the within-person (b = -0.08) - but not between-person - level.

Adequate-to-good fit was defined as Comparative Fit Index and Tucker Lewis Index > 0.90, Root Mean Square Error of Approximation < 0.08, and Standardized Root Mean Square Residuals < 0.08.

The emotion dysregulation factor mediated positive associations between the negative affect and feeling disconnected while eating factors at the within-person (b = 0.03) and between-person (b = 0.69) levels. There were also significant indirect effects at the within-person - but not between-person - level among the negative affect, emotion dysregulation, and (separately) general sense of LOC while eating, difficulties resisting eating, and feeling driven/compelled to eat factors (b = 0.02-0.03).

consequence.explanation: No APA-format test statistic exists to recompute, so statcheck's entire method is inapplicable to this paper.

findings.notes: Zero statistics found is the correct result, not a tool failure, and it carries information: the paper contains no t(df), F(df1,df2), r(df), chi-squared(df) or z anywhere in its prose. Its inferential content is expressed entirely as bare p-values and standardised betas in Table 2. The consequence is that the most standard automated consistency check in this toolkit cannot touch this paper at all -- the same underlying reporting gap as table2_coefficients_no_df, seen from a second direction.

findings.location: Participants and Procedures, first sentence of paragraph 2
findings.quote: The present study used baseline EMA data from a multisite randomized controlled trial (NCT0204349) testing the efficacy of Integrative Cognitive‐Affective Therapy (ICAT‐BED) versus guided self‐help Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Eating Disorders (CBTgsh).

consequence.explanation: The trial registration cannot be located from the identifier as printed, so a reader cannot check the parent trial's registered design or outcomes against this secondary analysis.

findings.notes: ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers are 'NCT' followed by eight digits; the printed string has seven, so it cannot resolve to any registration. No tool in this kit checks registry identifiers, so this is `manual` and capped at `suspicious`: no arithmetic was performed. I verified it by reading the string in both sources -- it appears identically in the published XML and on p. 6 of the author manuscript -- so it is a typographical error carried through production, not an extraction artifact. I have deliberately not guessed the intended number. This matters more than an ordinary typo because it sits in a load-bearing sentence: it is the paper's only pointer to the provenance and registered design of the data it analyses.

findings.location: Results, 'Emotion Dysregulation (M) to LOC Eating (Y)' paragraph, and Discussion, 'Variations Across LOC Eating Dimensions'
findings.quote: Specifically, there were significant positive associations between the emotion dysregulation factors relative to the general sense of LOC while eating and feelings of disconnection (e.g., numb, zoned out, on auto‐pilot) while eating factors at both the within‐person (β = 0.13–0.14) and between‐person (β = 0.68–0.77) levels.

computed.point_estimate_ordering: the 'non-significant' between-person coefficients (0.89, 0.85) are LARGER than the 'significant' one (0.82)

inputs.rows_compared: Table 2 Model 1 vs Model 3, between-person, direct and indirect

consequence.explanation: The paper's second stated aim -- that mediation 'varies across different LOC eating dimensions' -- is supported only by which side of alpha = .05 each separate test fell on, never by a test of the difference between dimensions.

findings.notes: No tool computed this; it is a reading of Table 2 against the paper's own conclusions, so it is `manual` and capped at `suspicious`. The headline claim of 'notable variations ... based on the LOC eating dimension' is drawn by comparing significance verdicts across six separately estimated models, and at the between-person level the contrast rests on p = .048 versus p = .055 -- with the point estimate of the NON-significant coefficient (0.89) larger than that of the significant one (0.82). This is the classic error of treating the difference between significant and non-significant as itself significant. The paper never reports a test of whether any two LOC dimensions differ, and since the six outcomes come from the same participants at the same moments, such a test is both possible and the appropriate way to support the claim. The Discussion nonetheless builds a substantive theoretical account on the contrast ('there may be certain stages of a LOC eating episode that may be precipitated by such a sequence'). The innocent reading is that this reflects conventional practice in the field rather than anything unusual to this paper; the consequence is that the novelty claim is weaker than stated.

findings.location: Figure 1, p. 19 of the author manuscript
findings.quote: Conceptual model depicting the associations of interest that were examined in the assessed multilevel structural equation models.

consequence.explanation: No statistic in this paper is reachable only through a figure, so the usual figure-blindness limitation does not apply here.

findings.notes: The paper's single figure is a path diagram with no axes and no plotted data -- it depicts model structure (lagging, levels, X/M/Y roles), not results. Recorded explicitly because 'we could not read the figures' is a standard caveat on these reviews and it is NOT a live gap for this paper: every number the paper reports is in its text or its two tables, all of which were read.

tables_checked: Table 1 (Participant characteristics) - 26 cells, 100% typed, 0 ambiguous, 36 checks run, 3 refused

Table 2 (Multilevel structural equation models) - 84 coefficients (b, SE, p, beta) across 6 models x 2 levels; 71 submitted to regression-batch, all indeterminate for want of df; 21 rows cross-checked against the PDF

unchecked.location: Data S1 / Supplement (referenced 9 times; not provided to this review)
unchecked.reason: The largest coverage gap in this review. Data S1 is stated to contain: the model fit statistics for all six MSEMs (the basis of 'All MSEMs exhibited good fit'), the multilevel confirmatory factor analyses confirming the factor structure of affect, emotion dysregulation and LOC eating, the missing-data analyses that justify controlling for survey number, the comparison of the 5 excluded against the 107 retained participants, and the ENTIRE set of exploratory analyses. None of it could be read. 'Present but not supplied' is not the same as 'absent' -- no supplementary file was among the inputs for this paper.

unchecked.location: Results, 'Exploratory Analyses' section
unchecked.reason: An entire results section reports significance verdicts for a second set of six MSEMs ('indirect effects were significant for models involving momentary emotion dysregulation (predictor), negative affect (mediator), and four LOC eating dimensions') with no coefficient, no standard error and no p-value anywhere in the main text. Nothing in it is checkable. It also means the paper's true multiple-comparison count is at least double the 12 tests per family I could enumerate.

unchecked.location: Table 1, BDI, CIA and DERS total-score rows (GRIMMER and SPRITE)
unchecked.reason: check_table refused these three cells by design: GRIMMER and SPRITE need a STATED scale maximum and the paper gives none for any of the three instruments. Falling back on the tool's default 1-7 Likert range would manufacture an impossibility out of ordinary total scores. The SD of the BDI row (exactly 10.00, paired with a mean of exactly 15.00) is the one value in Table 1 I would most like to have tested and could not.

unchecked.location: Table 2, all 84 coefficients
unchecked.reason: No degrees of freedom, no test statistic and no confidence interval are reported for any path, and the level-1 sample size (number of momentary eating-episode observations) is never given, so no reported p-value can be reconciled with its own b and SE. Additionally b and SE are printed to only two decimals, which for a coefficient such as -0.07 (0.03) leaves the implied p uncertain across a range that straddles .05.

unchecked.location: Results, paragraph 1, six LOC eating means and SDs
unchecked.reason: Six means and SDs are reported for the LOC eating dimensions with no n. The denominator is the number of surveys that followed an eating episode, which is never stated (it is a subset of the 3131 completed surveys). Without n, GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE cannot be run on any of them, even though these are single-item integer 1-5 responses and would otherwise be ideal candidates. Only the SD-range check, which needs no n, could be applied.

unchecked.location: Study Purpose, r = 0.948 between emotion dysregulation and negative urgency
unchecked.reason: Reported without n, df or confidence interval, and attributed to a prior analysis of the same sample (Wonderlich et al. 2024). It is within the logical bounds of a correlation, but no consistency check applies to a bare coefficient with no accompanying statistics. Worth noting substantively rather than forensically: at r = 0.948 this paper's mediator and the prior paper's mediator are very nearly the same variable.

unchecked.location: Table 2, standardised beta column (84 values)
unchecked.reason: The beta values cannot be independently verified against the unstandardised b without the latent factor variances at each level, which are not reported. They were read and recorded but no check was run on them.

unchecked.location: Whole paper, detect_duplication
unchecked.reason: Deliberately not run, and the reason matters. The paper has only ONE block of means and SDs (Table 1, a single sample), so there is no independent second block to compare against. In Table 2 the 'Negative affect to Emotion dysregulation' row repeats near-identically across all six models -- but this is EXPECTED, not duplication: the six models share the same predictor-to-mediator submodel on the same 107 participants and differ only in the outcome. Running the tool here would have flagged legitimate re-estimation as copy-paste. Supporting that reading, the between-person coefficient does vary across models (0.96, 0.96, 0.96, 0.95, 0.95, 0.95), exactly as re-estimation produces and copy-paste does not.

unchecked.location: Data Availability Statement
unchecked.reason: Not a finding, but recorded for the reader: data, materials and code are 'available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request' rather than deposited. This is an honest request-based statement rather than the 'all data are included' pattern rulebook rule 7 flags, but combined with the unavailable Data S1 it means none of the paper's fit statistics, factor analyses or exploratory results could be independently examined from published materials.
